idiom_name: per-instance attribute attachment plus typing.Protocol checks or a weakref.WeakKeyDictionary side table
implementation_notes: A Python instance keeps its attributes in __dict__: doc.spell_state = state attaches the attribute without touching the class, and hasattr/getattr (or isinstance against a runtime_checkable Protocol) is the capability query - the language absorbs the pattern for ordinary classes. The classic registry returns only where attribute attachment is impossible: objects with __slots__, built-in types (int, str, list) and C-extension instances reject new attributes, and objects that override __getattr__/__setattr__ can misreport or swallow them. There the canonical replacement is a side table - weakref.WeakKeyDictionary, whose documentation says it 'can be used to associate additional data with an object owned by other parts of an application without adding attributes to those objects ... especially useful with objects that override attribute accesses'. Use abc.ABCMeta.register when the subject should be recognised as a virtual subclass of an extension interface without changing its base classes, and key an explicit registry by the Protocol/ABC object rather than by a string.
pitfalls: __slots__, built-ins and many C-extension types refuse new attributes, and __getattr__/__setattr__ overrides can make attachment appear to succeed while storing nothing - wrap direct setattr in try/except AttributeError or use the side table from the start.

A plain dict keyed by an object both keeps the object alive for the life of the dict and compares by equality, so two equal-but-distinct subjects collapse into one entry; WeakKeyDictionary keys are weak (they disappear with the object) but must be weak-referenceable, so dicts, lists and tuples raise TypeError as keys.

Attribute attachment is not atomic with respect to readers: another thread iterating __dict__ or hasattr during attachment sees a half-initialised extension, and a weak side table can lose an entry while a strong reference to the value is what keeps the state alive - keep the extension's lifetime explicit.
